name: Grounding / earthing mat

lead: Grounding or earthing products are conductive mats, sheets or bands that plug into a wall socket's ground port or a ground rod. People sleep on them hoping for deeper sleep and less inflammation, which they connect to a fresher, more rested appearance.

Proponents say electrons from the earth's surface neutralise free radicals in the body. Encyclopedic sources list earthing as an alternative medicine practice, and no clinical trials were retrieved for sleep or appearance outcomes.

paras: Users lay the mat on the bed or desk, or wear a band, and connect it to the ground port of a wall outlet or to a ground rod. It is typically used nightly as part of a sleep setup. Users describe judging the effect over weeks of sleep quality.

The product is a passive conductive fabric, but connecting through a wall outlet raises electrical-safety questions that manufacturers address with built-in resistors. The sources reviewed provide no safety data. Checking that the outlet is properly grounded is a commonly stated precaution.

angle.text: Users sleep on conductive sheets and mats connected to the earth, hoping for better sleep and wellbeing and so a more rested look. Proponents say earth contact neutralises free radicals; it is listed as an alternative medicine practice and trials were not found.

lead: Grounding, also called earthing, is the practice of making direct contact with the earth, or with conductive products wired to it, on the belief that this benefits health. Grounding mats, sheets and patches are conductive fabrics that connect to the ground port of a wall socket or to a ground rod, so the user can stay connected while sleeping or sitting at a desk.[1]

People who use them are mostly after better sleep, lower stress and less soreness, and in appearance-focused circles the pitch is the downstream payoff: sounder sleep and recovery are said to show up as a more rested face, calmer skin and more energy for training. Proponents also describe lower inflammation, which they link to skin and recovery.[2][3]

Research on grounding is small. A 2019 randomized trial in 16 massage therapists at a wellness centre examined grounding, pain and quality of life,[4] and reviews written by grounding advocates summarise earlier work on inflammation, sleep and pain.[2][3] Wikipedia lists earthing as an alternative medicine practice.[1] No study cited here has tested grounding mats against facial appearance.
infobox: Wall-outlet ground port or ground rod

paras: Products are conductive mats, sheets and patches meant to connect the user to the earth's potential, usually via a wall outlet ground.[1] Barefoot contact with soil, grass or sand is the original form of the practice and is the form most trials describe.[4]

Proponents propose that contact with the earth lets electrons from the ground neutralise free radicals in the body, reducing inflammation, and a 2023 article in the Biomedical Journal calls grounding a possible anti-inflammatory approach.[2] A 2020 review in Explore argues that earthing should be part of integrative and lifestyle medicine and collects research evidence and clinical observations in support.[3]
Wikipedia classes the practice under alternative medicine.[1] The sources cited here include advocacy-oriented reviews rather than large independent trials.

A randomized controlled trial published in 2019 in Explore enrolled sixteen massage therapists (mean age 42.8) at the Chopra Center in California to test the effects of grounding on pain and quality of life.[4] Reviews of the grounding literature summarise small studies on inflammation, sleep and pain.[2][3] No studies found that test grounding mats for skin or facial appearance.

Grounding is mentioned only occasionally on looksmax.org. One thread praises walking barefoot on grass and stone, saying shoes and socks feel constricting, and a reply jokes that you are taller barefoot.[5] Posts about grounding techniques for anxiety, a different use of the word, also circulate there.[6]

lore.intro: Grounding in looksmaxxing spaces is mostly barefoot-outdoors enthusiasm and passing mentions; mats are marketed with sleep and inflammation claims.[5][2]
